linkedin_version:
Payday Super Is Now a Cash-Flow Readiness Issue (And Lenders Are Watching)

For SME owners planning to borrow, Payday Super is not just payroll admin. It changes how payroll, super, tax and working-capital rhythm may be read in a lender-style cash-flow story.

**What changed (July 1, 2026):**
Super moved from quarterly to payday. For most businesses, that means:
- More frequent super payments (fortnightly/monthly vs quarterly)
- Higher short-term working capital needs
- Changed cash-flow rhythm
- New data points for lenders to assess

**What lenders see:**
Before: Quarterly super (delayed payments were common, somewhat tolerated)
Now: Payday super (monthly/fortnightly timing signals — delays are red flags)

**Why this matters for borrowing:**
Lenders assess super timing as part of your cash-flow discipline story. Consistent, on-time Payday Super payments signal:
✓ Working capital is sufficient
✓ Business adapted well to new rhythm
✓ Cash-flow management is proactive (not reactive)

Late or irregular super timing (even in the new system) signals:
❌ Working capital stress
❌ Cash-flow unpredictability
❌ Business struggling to adapt

**The lending assessment question:**
"Did this business adjust its working capital correctly for Payday Super, or is it cash-flow stressed?"

**Before you apply, know where you stand.**

Our Commercial Financial Health Check assesses your cash-flow readiness in the post-Payday Super environment — 4 minutes, no credit check, with clear insights into what lenders will see.
